## Week 9 goals {#sec-week09-goals .smaller}

::: notes
Before this slide: about 15 minutes on the Gauss-Markov assumptions, from the week 8 deck.
Then read the goals aloud and come back to them at the end.
Goals 3 and 4 matter most for the exam.
:::

By the end of today, you will be able to:

1. Explain **Simpson's paradox**: why an association in pooled data can point the opposite way from the association within groups.
2. Say what **controlling for a variable** does, with Venn diagrams of shared variation, and read each coefficient as a **partial association**, including a **dummy variable**.
3. Use a **DAG** to justify control variables, and recognise controls that do harm.
4. Compare models by how well they predict new data, using **leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO)**.
5. Report several models in one **regression table**, built with `broom.mixed` and `kable()`.

# A puzzle {#sec-puzzle}

## Does education pay? {#sec-does-education-pay .smaller}

::: notes
Ask first, before the reveal: one more year of schooling, higher or lower income?
Take a show of hands.
Almost everyone will say higher.
Then reveal the figure and let it sink in.
:::

We have survey data on 200 working adults: years of schooling and annual income, in thousand EUR.

> **Q:** Predict the sign: does a person with more schooling earn more or less, on average?

. . .


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(income, aes(x = education, y = income)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey40", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = col_3, linewidth = 1.2) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = "Years of schooling",
    y = "Annual income (thousand EUR)",
    title = "More schooling, less income?"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Annual income against years of schooling for all 200 people, with the least-squares line drawn for the eye. In the pooled data, people with more schooling earn less.](week09_files/figure-revealjs/fig-pooled-1.png){#fig-pooled width=5000}
:::
:::


## Should you drop out? {#sec-drop-out .smaller}

::: notes
Ask: should you advise a friend to leave school, based on this line?
Collect answers, then reveal the colours.
The lines within each group rise, the pooled line falls.
Do not explain yet, ask the room why first.
:::

In the pooled data, every extra year of schooling goes with **1.5 thousand EUR less** income.

> **Q:** Would you advise a friend to leave school early?

. . .


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(income, aes(x = education, y = income, colour = gender)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = gender_cols) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = "Years of schooling",
    y = "Annual income (thousand EUR)",
    colour = NULL,
    title = "Within each group, schooling pays"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The same 200 people, coloured by gender, with one least-squares line per group. Within each gender, more schooling goes with more income. The pooled line of the previous figure runs the other way.](week09_files/figure-revealjs/fig-by-gender-1.png){#fig-by-gender width=5000}
:::
:::


## Simpson's paradox {#sec-simpson .smaller}

::: notes
Let the room explain it before revealing the two bullets.
The data are synthetic and exaggerated on purpose, so the mechanism is easy to see.
The pattern itself is real and common: Berkeley admissions is the classic case.
Close with the two questions, they structure the next two sections.
:::

An association in the pooled data can **reverse** inside every group.
This is **Simpson's paradox** [@simpson1951interpretation; @pearl2016causal].

. . .

Why here?

- In these data, **women have 4.2 more years of schooling** than men on average.
- And **women earn less** than men with the same schooling, a gap of 19 thousand EUR.

So gender is related to **both** schooling and income, and the pooled line mixes the two.

. . .

Two questions follow:

1. **Venn diagrams:** what does it mean to "hold gender constant"?
2. **DAGs:** how do we know *which* variables to hold constant?

# What controlling means {#sec-venn}

## Shared variation {#sec-venn-two .smaller}

::: notes
Each circle is the variation of one variable: how much it differs between people.
The overlap is variation the two share: where people differ in schooling, they also differ in income.
A regression slope is learned from exactly that overlap.
This picture goes back to Kennedy, who called it the Ballentine.
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tibble(
  name = c("Income", "Schooling"),
  x0 = c(0, 1.3),
  y0 = c(0, 0),
  r = 1,
  lx = c(-0.4, 1.7),
  ly = c(0, 0),
  fill = c(col_1, col_2)
) |>
  draw_venn(
    regions = tibble(x = 0.65, y = 0, label = "A"),
    title = "Two variables"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Each circle stands for the variation of one variable across people. The overlap is the variation income and schooling share, and it is what the bivariate slope learns from.](week09_files/figure-revealjs/fig-venn-two-1.png){#fig-venn-two width=2200}
:::
:::

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
- Each **circle** is the variation of one variable: how much people differ on it.
- The **overlap A** is variation the two share.
- The bivariate model learns its slope from **A**, and only from **A** [@kennedy1981ballentine].

> **Q:** Gender is related to both, so where would its circle go?
:::

::::

## Adding a control {#sec-venn-three .smaller}

::: notes
Walk the regions slowly.
A: schooling and income vary together, and gender is not involved.
B: all three vary together, so we cannot tell whether schooling or gender moves income.
The naive model uses A and B, and credits all of it to schooling.
The controlled model uses only A for the schooling slope.
That is all "holding gender constant" means: compare people within one colour of the earlier figure.
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
venn_three <- tibble(
  name = c("Income", "Schooling", "Gender"),
  x0 = c(0, 1.3, 0.65),
  y0 = c(0, 0, -1.1),
  r = 1,
  lx = c(-0.45, 1.75, 0.65),
  ly = c(0.3, 0.3, -1.6),
  fill = c(col_1, col_2, col_3)
)
draw_venn(
  venn_three,
  regions = tibble(
    x = c(0.65, 0.65, 0.1, 1.2),
    y = c(0.45, -0.3, -0.8, -0.8),
    label = c("A", "B", "C", "D")
  ),
  title = "Three variables"
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Gender added as a third circle. Region B is variation all three share. The naive model credits A and B to schooling, the controlled model learns the schooling slope from A only.](week09_files/figure-revealjs/fig-venn-three-1.png){#fig-venn-three width=2200}
:::
:::

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.small}
| Region | Shared by | Used for the schooling slope by |
|---|---|---|
| A | income, schooling | both models |
| B | all three | the naive model only |
| C | income, gender | neither |
| D | schooling, gender | neither |

: The regions of @fig-venn-three and which model uses each to learn the schooling slope. {#tbl-venn-regions}
:::

**Controlling for gender** means learning the schooling slope from variation that gender does not share.
In @fig-by-gender: comparing people **within one colour**.
:::

::::

## When controls overlap {#sec-venn-collinear .smaller}

::: notes
Ask before revealing the figure.
Answer: A shrinks to almost nothing, so there is little information left about the schooling slope.
This is A4 from the recap, which was trivial with one predictor.
Perfect overlap means no information at all, near-perfect overlap means a very wide posterior.
In our data schooling and gender correlate strongly, so expect a wider posterior for the slope once gender is in.
Then the callout: the Venn diagram shows which variation is used, never signs or causes.
:::

> **Q:** What if the schooling and gender circles overlapped almost completely?

. . .

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tibble(
  name = c("Income", "Schooling", "Gender"),
  x0 = c(0, 1.3, 1.35),
  y0 = c(0, 0, -0.1),
  r = 1,
  lx = c(-0.45, 1.3, 1.6),
  ly = c(0.3, 1.15, -1.3),
  fill = c(col_1, col_2, col_3)
) |>
  draw_venn(
    regions = tibble(x = 0.53, y = 0.55, label = "A"),
    title = "Nearly collinear"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Schooling and gender almost coincide. Little variation in schooling is left that gender does not share, so region A, the information about the schooling slope, is tiny.](week09_files/figure-revealjs/fig-venn-collinear-1.png){#fig-venn-collinear width=2200}
:::
:::

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
- Region A is tiny, so the data say **little** about the schooling slope, and its posterior is **wide**.
- In full overlap, A vanishes: the slope cannot be learned at all.
- This is **A4, no perfect collinearity**, from the recap, which only bites once there are several predictors.
:::

::::

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
**The circles show which variation a coefficient uses, nothing more.**
They cannot show signs, so they cannot show the reversal itself.
Which circles belong in the model at all is a question for theory: DAGs.
:::

# Which controls {#sec-dags}

## A DAG organises the theory {#sec-dag-ours .smaller}

::: notes
A DAG is drawn before step 3, and it is not yet a model.
It says which variables are related and in which direction, never how: no shape, no size, no sign.
Step 3 then formalises it: the arrows into income become terms in the linear predictor.
Walk the three arrows of our DAG and ask for the story behind each.
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- A **directed acyclic graph (DAG)** writes down what we *theorise* before we write the model [@mcelreath2020rethinking-ch6].
- **Nodes** are variables, **arrows** say which variable influences which.
- A DAG says **whether** and in **which direction**, not **how**: no shape, no size, no sign.
- **Acyclic:** no path leads back to where it started.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
draw_dag(
  nodes = tibble(
    name = c("G", "E", "I"),
    x = c(1, 0, 2),
    y = c(1, 0, 0),
    label = c("Gender", "Schooling", "Income")
  ),
  edges = tibble(from = c("G", "G", "E"), to = c("E", "I", "I")),
  title = "Our theory"
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Our theory as a DAG: gender influences schooling and income, and schooling influences income.](week09_files/figure-revealjs/fig-dag-ours-1.png){#fig-dag-ours width=2200}
:::
:::

:::

::::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
**Draw the DAG first, then formalise.**
Every arrow into the outcome becomes a term at step 3, and the model decides how large.
:::

## Three ways variables connect {#sec-dag-types .smaller}

::: notes
Fork: a common cause, like gender in our story.
Leaving it out mixes its influence into the slope, which is the puzzle.
Pipe: the path runs through M, so controlling for M removes part of the very association we want.
Collider: two arrows collide in C.
X and Y are unrelated, but controlling for C makes them look related.
Then the question: ask for one example of each from the room before the next slide.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dag_fork <- draw_dag(
  tibble(
    name = c("Z", "X", "Y"),
    x = c(1, 0, 2),
    y = c(1, 0, 0),
    label = c("Z", "X", "Y")
  ),
  tibble(from = c("Z", "Z"), to = c("X", "Y")),
  title = "Fork: Z is a confounder"
)
dag_pipe <- draw_dag(
  tibble(
    name = c("X", "M", "Y"),
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = 0,
    label = c("X", "M", "Y")
  ),
  tibble(from = c("X", "M"), to = c("M", "Y")),
  title = "Pipe: M is a mediator"
)
dag_collider <- draw_dag(
  tibble(
    name = c("X", "Y", "C"),
    x = c(0, 2, 1),
    y = c(1, 1, 0),
    label = c("X", "Y", "C")
  ),
  tibble(from = c("X", "Y"), to = c("C", "C")),
  title = "Collider: C is caused by both"
)
dag_fork | dag_pipe | dag_collider
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The three basic structures. In a fork, Z is a common cause of X and Y. In a pipe, X influences Y through M. In a collider, X and Y both influence C.](week09_files/figure-revealjs/fig-dag-types-1.png){#fig-dag-types width=5000}
:::
:::


::: {.small}
| Structure | Control for the middle variable? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Fork (confounder) | **Yes** | Otherwise its influence is credited to X |
| Pipe (mediator) | **Usually not** | It removes part of the association we want |
| Collider | **Never** | It creates an association that is not there |

: Whether to control for the middle variable of each structure in @fig-dag-types. {#tbl-dag-rules}
:::

> **Q:** Which structure is gender in our story, and which is the job someone holds (occupation)?

## Collider bias: a control that lies {#sec-collider .smaller}



::: notes
Gender is a fork, so we control for it.
Occupation is a pipe: schooling gets you a job that pays, so controlling for it removes part of the return to schooling.
Now the collider, as a story.
An elite programme admits people with good grades or good connections.
Grades and connections are unrelated in the population.
Among those admitted, they are negatively related: whoever got in with weak grades must have had strong connections.
Controlling for admission, or studying only the admitted, does exactly this.
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(applicants, aes(x = grades, y = connections)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = admitted), alpha = 0.6, size = 1.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_smooth(
    data = filter(applicants, admitted),
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    colour = col_2
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = col_2),
    labels = c("Rejected", "Admitted")
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = "Grades",
    y = "Connections",
    colour = NULL,
    title = "Selected on both"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Five hundred simulated applicants. Grades and connections are unrelated overall (grey line), but negatively related among the admitted (orange).](week09_files/figure-revealjs/fig-collider-1.png){#fig-collider width=2600}
:::
:::

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
An elite programme admits on good **grades** or good **connections**, unrelated in the population.

- All applicants: correlation **-0.02**.
- Admitted only: correlation **-0.64**.

Admission is a **collider**:

grades $\rightarrow$ admitted $\leftarrow$ connections

Controlling for it creates the association.
:::

::::

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
**Every control variable is a claim, and it needs a justification.**
More controls are not safer: a mediator removes part of the association you want, a collider invents one.
:::

# The eight steps, two models {#sec-eight-steps}

## Step 1: Estimand {#sec-step1 .smaller}

::: notes
The key word is "same gender".
The estimand changes when the set of controls changes, so the controls belong to step 1, not to step 5.
Then the warning, once and firmly.
:::

The research question:

> Is schooling associated with income, among people of the same gender?

. . .

What precisely do we want to learn?

> How much higher, on average, is the income of a person with one more year of schooling, **compared with a person of the same gender**?

. . .

That is a **partial association**: a slope that holds gender constant.
The controls are part of the estimand, so they are chosen here, at step 1, with the DAG.

. . .

::: {.callout-warning}
**A partial association is still not a causal effect.**
It is a causal effect only if the DAG is right and complete, and the data cannot check that.
Ability, family background or field of study could all still be missing.
:::

## Step 2: Data summary {#sec-step2 .smaller}

::: notes
Our first computed table today: group, summarise, kable.
Ask: which row explains the puzzle?
Women have more schooling and lower income, both.
:::


::: {#tbl-by-gender .cell tbl-cap='Number of people, mean years of schooling and mean annual income by gender. Women have more schooling on average, and a lower average income.'}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="false"}
income |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    schooling = mean(education),
    income = mean(income)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 1,
    col.names = c("Gender", "People", "Schooling (years)", "Income (thousand EUR)")
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Gender | People| Schooling (years)| Income (thousand EUR)|
|:------|------:|-----------------:|---------------------:|
|Man    |    112|              12.1|                  37.8|
|Woman  |     88|              16.3|                  25.8|


:::
:::


## Step 2: One variable at a time {#sec-step2-univariate .smaller}

::: notes
Ask before pointing at anything: what does gender do to each distribution?
Women sit to the right on schooling and to the left on income.
Pooled, the two groups blur into one wide hump.
That is the puzzle again, one variable at a time.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
income |>
  select(gender, education, income) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(education, income),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    variable = case_match(
      variable,
      "education" ~ "Years of schooling",
      "income" ~ "Annual income (thousand EUR)"
    ),
    variable = fct_relevel(variable, "Years of schooling")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = gender)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 20,
    position = "identity",
    alpha = 0.5,
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = gender_cols) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "People",
    fill = NULL,
    title = "Schooling and income, by gender"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Years of schooling and annual income, one histogram per gender. Women have more schooling and a lower income, so each variable consists of two shifted groups.](week09_files/figure-revealjs/fig-univariate-1.png){#fig-univariate width=5000}
:::
:::


> **Q:** What does gender do to each distribution?

. . .

Together with @fig-by-gender: schooling and income rise together **within** each gender, and gender is related to **both**.

## Step 3: Formal model {#sec-step3 .smaller}

::: notes
The same template as week 8: outcome distribution, then linear predictor.
New: one term per predictor in the linear predictor.
x for every predictor: x1 is schooling, x2 is gender, and the second subscript numbers the predictor.
Centring: x1 is schooling minus 12, so the intercept is the expected income of a man with 12 years, a person in our data, which we can defend a prior for.
The naive model is the same model without the gender term.
:::

**1. Outcome distribution.**
Income is drawn from a normal distribution with mean $\mu_i$ and standard deviation $\sigma$:

$$
y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma)
$$ {#eq-likelihood}

**2. Linear predictor.**
The mean is a straight line in schooling, shifted by gender:

$$
\mu_i = \alpha + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2}
$$ {#eq-linear-predictor}

::: {.small}
- $y_i$ is the income of person $i$, in thousand EUR.
- $x_{i1}$ is their years of schooling **minus 12**, so 0 means 12 years and 4 means 16 years.
- $x_{i2}$ is 1 for a woman and 0 for a man.
- The **naive model** is the same, without $\beta_2 x_{i2}$.
:::

Read $\sim$ as **is drawn from** (random) and $=$ as **is defined as** (fixed).

. . .

$\beta_1$ is a **partial association**: the difference in expected income between two people of the **same gender** whose schooling differs by one year.

## Step 3: Why subtract 12? {#sec-centring .smaller}

::: notes
Ask first: what would alpha mean if x1 were plain years of schooling?
Answer: the expected income of a man with no schooling at all, far outside our data, so nobody could defend a prior for it.
Centring fixes that and changes nothing else: the slope is the same.
In R this is one mutate, at step 5.
:::

The intercept $\alpha$ is the expected income when **every predictor is 0**.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.small}
| Years of schooling | $x_{i1}$ |
|---:|---:|
| 8 | $-4$ |
| 12 | 0 |
| 16 | 4 |
| 20 | 8 |

: Years of schooling and the centred predictor $x_{i1}$, which subtracts 12. {#tbl-centring}
:::
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
- With plain years, $x_{i1} = 0$ would be a person with **no schooling at all**, far outside our data.
- Centred at 12, $x_{i1} = 0$ is a person with **12 years**, so $\alpha$ is the expected income of a man with 12 years of schooling.
:::

::::

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
**Centring moves only the intercept.**
The slope $\beta_1$ stays the same, and now $\alpha$ is a value we can defend a prior for.
:::

## Step 3: A dummy variable {#sec-dummy .smaller}

::: notes
A dummy is a 0 or 1 variable, and its coefficient is a shift of the intercept.
Men are the reference group: for them the term is zero.
With more than two categories, one dummy per category except the reference, and brms builds them from a factor.
The callout matters for next week: the lines are parallel because we assumed it.
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
$x_{i2}$ is a **dummy variable**: 1 for women, 0 for men, the **reference group**.

- Men: $\mu_i = \alpha + \beta_1 x_{i1}$
- Women: $\mu_i = (\alpha + \beta_2) + \beta_1 x_{i1}$

$\beta_2$ **shifts the line**: the expected income gap between a woman and a man with the same schooling.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
expand_grid(education = c(8, 20), gender = c("Man", "Woman")) |>
  mutate(
    mu = 38 + 1.6 * (education - 12) - 18 * (gender == "Woman")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = mu, colour = gender)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = 16,
    xend = 16,
    y = 38 + 1.6 * 4,
    yend = 38 + 1.6 * 4 - 18,
    arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.15, "cm")),
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 16.9, y = 35.4, label = "beta[2]", parse = TRUE, size = 5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = gender_cols) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = "Years of schooling",
    y = "Expected income",
    colour = NULL,
    title = "One slope, two intercepts"
  )
```

![What the linear predictor of the controlled model implies, with illustrative values. The dummy shifts the line for women by beta 2. Both lines share the slope beta 1.](week09_files/figure-revealjs/fig-dummy-1.png){#fig-dummy width=2400}
:::
:::

:::

::::

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
**The lines are parallel because the model says so.**
Whether schooling pays off differently for women and men is next week: interactions.
:::

## Step 3: The posterior {#sec-step3-posterior .smaller}

::: notes
Read the left side first: these are all the unknowns.
Count them out loud: four parameters, so four priors.
The naive model has three.
:::

**3. Posterior, proportional form.**

$$
P(\alpha, \beta_1, \beta_2, \sigma \mid \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{X}) \propto \mathcal{L}(\alpha, \beta_1, \beta_2, \sigma \mid \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{X}) \times P(\alpha) \, P(\beta_1) \, P(\beta_2) \, P(\sigma)
$$ {#eq-posterior}

- $\mathbf{y}$ is the income column, and $\mathbf{X}$ holds the two predictor columns, $\mathbf{x}_1$ (schooling) and $\mathbf{x}_2$ (gender), 200 rows each.
- The likelihood $\mathcal{L}$ comes from @eq-likelihood and @eq-linear-predictor, applied to every person.

. . .

The left side lists every unknown: **four parameters, so four priors** to choose.
The naive model has three.

## Step 3: The complete model {#sec-model-card .smaller}

::: notes
The card is the course format for step 3, as in week 8.
Read it top to bottom: the outcome, its mean, then one prior per unknown.
Open one details block live, the rest are for reading at home.
:::

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_i &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma) && \text{outcome distribution} \\
\mu_i &= \alpha + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} && \text{linear predictor} \\
\alpha &\sim \mathcal{N}(35, 10) && \text{prior} \\
\beta_1 &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 3) && \text{prior} \\
\beta_2 &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10) && \text{prior} \\
\sigma &\sim \text{Exponential}(0.1) && \text{prior}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-model}

Every prior is argued on the scale of the outcome, thousand EUR per year:

::: {.small}
<details>
<summary>The intercept, $\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(35, 10)$</summary>

::: {.callout-note}
**The expected income of a man with 12 years of schooling.**
Typical full-time incomes lie in the tens of thousands, so the prior is centred on 35.
With 95 percent probability it lies between 15 and 55.
:::

</details>

<details>
<summary>The schooling slope, $\beta_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 3)$</summary>

::: {.callout-note}
**Centred on no association, because the sign is what we want to learn.**
An extra year of schooling could plausibly shift income by a few thousand EUR.
95 percent of the prior lies between $-6$ and $+6$.
:::

</details>

<details>
<summary>The gender dummy, $\beta_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10)$</summary>

::: {.callout-note}
**Centred on no gap, open in both directions.**
A gap of 20 thousand EUR at the same schooling would be very large.
95 percent of the prior lies between $-20$ and $+20$.
:::

</details>

<details>
<summary>The residual standard deviation, $\sigma \sim \text{Exponential}(0.1)$</summary>

::: {.callout-note}
**Positive, and typically around 10.**
An exponential with rate 0.1 has a mean of 10 thousand EUR, so people typically lie that far from their expected income, and smaller values are more plausible than larger ones.
:::

</details>
:::

The naive model uses the same priors for $\alpha$, $\beta_1$ and $\sigma$.

## Step 4: Prior predictive check {#sec-step4 .smaller}

::: notes
Narrate if behind.
Lines are average worlds, one per prior draw.
Some slopes are steep and some intercepts low, a few lines dip below zero, which is mild.
The priors allow both signs of the slope and a wide range of gaps, which is what we want.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
tibble(
  draw = 1:50,
  alpha = rnorm(50, 35, 10),
  beta_1 = rnorm(50, 0, 3),
  beta_2 = rnorm(50, 0, 10)
) |>
  expand_grid(education = c(8, 20), gender = c("Man", "Woman")) |>
  mutate(
    mu = alpha + beta_1 * (education - 12) + beta_2 * (gender == "Woman")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = mu, group = draw)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(colour = col_3, alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~gender) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = "Years of schooling",
    y = "Expected income (thousand EUR)",
    title = "Average worlds our priors consider possible"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Fifty lines per gender drawn from the priors of the controlled model. The priors allow rising and falling lines and gaps in both directions, all within a broadly plausible range of incomes.](week09_files/figure-revealjs/fig-prior-lines-1.png){#fig-prior-lines width=5000}

## Step 5: Fit both models {#sec-step5 .smaller}

::: notes
The two calls differ by one term in the formula and one prior.
The first line centres schooling: the edu12 column is x1 from the card.
0 + Intercept keeps the intercept at x1 = 0 and x2 = 0, so the prior on alpha means what the card says.
The LOO criterion is stored with each fit, for the comparison in a moment.
:::

::: {.small}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="false"}

shared_priors <- c(
  prior(normal(35, 10), class = "b", coef = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 3), class = "b", coef = "edu12"),
  prior(exponential(0.1), class = "sigma")
)

fit_naive <- brm(
  income ~ 0 + Intercept + edu12,
  data = income,
  prior = shared_priors,
  seed = 2026,
  refresh = 0,
  file = here("website", "slides", "data", "week09-fit-naive"),
  file_refit = "on_change"
)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="false"}
fit_gender <- brm(
  income ~ 0 + Intercept + edu12 + woman,
  data = income,
  prior = c(shared_priors, prior(normal(0, 10), class = "b", coef = "woman")),
  seed = 2026,
  refresh = 0,
  file = here("website", "slides", "data", "week09-fit-gender"),
  file_refit = "on_change"
)

fit_naive <- add_criterion(fit_naive, "loo")
fit_gender <- add_criterion(fit_gender, "loo")
```

# Comparing models {#sec-compare}



## Which model fits better? {#sec-which-fits .smaller}

::: notes
Ask first, take two or three answers.
Someone will say: the one closer to the data.
Answer: every added predictor brings a model closer to the data it was fitted on, even pure noise.
We want to know how well it predicts people it has not seen.
LOO does that by leaving each person out in turn.
Refitting 200 times would be slow, PSIS approximates it from the one fit we already have.
:::

> **Q:** We have two fitted models, so how would you decide which fits the data better?

. . .

- Every extra predictor brings a model **closer to the data it was fitted on**, even a predictor that is pure noise.
- What we want: how well does the model predict **people it has not seen**?

## Leave-one-out cross-validation {#sec-loo .smaller}

::: notes
Three steps, then the formula is only step 3 written down.
Higher ELPD means the model found the left-out people more plausible.
:::

**Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO)** asks exactly that:

1. Leave out person $i$, and fit the model to everyone else.
2. Ask how plausible the model finds person $i$'s actual income.
3. Repeat for every person and add up:

$$
\text{elpd}_{\text{loo}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log p(y_i \mid \mathbf{y}_{-i})
$$ {#eq-elpd}

The **expected log predictive density (ELPD)**: higher is better.
`loo()` approximates all $n$ refits from the one fit we already have [@vehtari2017practical].

## Comparing our two models {#sec-loo-compare .smaller}

::: notes
Read the table: the best model is the first row, with a difference of zero.
The second row says how much worse the other model predicts, and how uncertain that difference is.
Rule of thumb: a difference below about 4 is small, beyond that compare it with its standard error.
Here it is many standard errors, so the controlled model predicts clearly better.
Pareto k values below 0.7 mean the approximation can be trusted.
:::


::: {#tbl-loo .cell tbl-cap='LOO comparison of the two models. The better model comes first, with a difference of zero. The second row gives how much lower its ELPD is, and the standard error of that difference.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
loo_compare(fit_gender, fit_naive) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(
    model = case_match(
      model,
      "fit_gender" ~ "Controlling for gender",
      "fit_naive" ~ "Naive"
    )
  ) |>
  select(model, elpd_diff, se_diff) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 1,
    col.names = c("Model", "ELPD difference", "Standard error")
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Model                  | ELPD difference| Standard error|
|:----------------------|---------------:|--------------:|
|Controlling for gender |             0.0|            0.0|
|Naive                  |           -82.9|            9.6|


:::
:::


. . .

- The naive model predicts worse by **82.9**, with a standard error of 9.6.
- A difference below about **4** is small, and beyond that we compare it with its standard error: here it is **9 standard errors**.
- Largest Pareto $k$: 0.23, below 0.7, so the approximation can be trusted.

## What LOO cannot tell you {#sec-loo-limits .smaller}

::: notes
This is the most important slide of the section.
Ask: in the collider example, would adding admission as a predictor improve prediction of connections?
Yes, it would, and it would also produce a spurious association.
So LOO is a check of prediction, and the DAG is the argument for the estimand.
:::

> **Q:** In the admissions example, would a model predicting connections from grades **and admission** predict better than one from grades alone?

. . .

Yes: admission carries information about connections.
And it would show a negative association between grades and connections that is not there.

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
**LOO ranks how well models predict, not whether their controls are right.**
A collider or a mediator can improve the ELPD and still bias the coefficient you care about.
The DAG chooses the model for the estimand, and LOO checks how well it predicts.
:::

    aes(x = education, y = income, colour = gender),

## The marginal effect, before and after {#sec-marginal .smaller}



::: notes
This is the puzzle again, now as two posteriors.
Same data, same priors, one term more, and the posterior moves to the other side of zero.
The controlled posterior is wider: the Venn region A is smaller than A plus B.
Ask which one answers our estimand.
The controlled one, because the estimand said same gender.
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bind_rows(
  tibble(model = "Naive", beta = beta_naive),
  tibble(model = "Controlling for gender", beta = beta_gender)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = beta, fill = model)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, colour = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(Naive = "grey50", `Controlling for gender` = col_3)
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = "Thousand EUR per year of schooling",
    y = "Density",
    fill = NULL,
    title = "One term changes the answer"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Posteriors of the schooling slope in both models. Without gender, the slope is negative. Holding gender constant, it is positive and slightly wider. This is Simpson's paradox, seen in the posterior.](week09_files/figure-revealjs/fig-marginal-1.png){#fig-marginal width=2750}
:::
:::

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Naive:** -1.5 per year, 90 percent interval [-1.82, -1.19].

**Controlling for gender:** comparing two people of the same gender, one more year of schooling is associated with **1.57 thousand EUR** more income, 90 percent interval [1.19, 1.96].

**100 percent** of that posterior lies above zero.

## Step 8: Limitations {#sec-step8 .smaller}

::: notes
Ask the room for one limitation before revealing.
The last bullet leads straight into next week.
:::

- **Synthetic data:** built to show the paradox clearly, so the sizes are exaggerated.
- **The DAG may be incomplete:** ability, family background or field of study could still confound schooling and income.
- **Gender as a binary dummy:** a simplification of the measurement.
- **Additive by assumption:** one schooling slope for everyone, so the model cannot yet say whether it differs by gender.

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
**A control fixes one bias, the one the DAG names.**
Naming what the model still cannot rule out is part of the answer.
:::

# Appendix {#sec-appendix}

## Appendix: how large the reversal is {#sec-ovb .smaller}

::: notes
Not exam material.
The pooled slope is the within-gender slope plus a bias term, and the bias term is the gender gap times how strongly gender tracks schooling.
:::

::: {.small}
If income truly depends on schooling $x_1$ and gender $x_2$, a model with schooling alone finds, in large samples,

$$
\beta^{\text{pooled}} = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \cdot \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2)}{\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{x}_1)}
$$ {#eq-ovb}

The second term is the **omitted variable bias**: the gender gap $\beta_2$, times how much the share of women rises per year of schooling.

For our data, with least-squares values: $1.62 + (-18.77) \times 0.166 = -1.5$, which is the pooled slope of -1.5 in @fig-pooled.

The bias is large because both factors are: a big gap, and a strong link between gender and schooling.
A control matters only where **both** of its arrows in the DAG are strong.
:::
